events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Omar proposes Omar, Arjun. I know I am good; with no other information, I choose Arjun as the second member.

I have no information yet that would make me object to Omar and Arjun. Omar's reasoning is clear enough for a first mission, and we all have the same limited information. I'm willing to back this team unless someone raises a concrete concern. Let's hear any objections before we vote.

I support the proposed team of Omar and Arjun for Mission 1. As a Loyal Servant I hold no private information about anyone, so my view of each player is formed only by what I observe publicly at the table. With five players and a two-person team, the proposal is simply the leader and one other member, and Omar's stated reasoning is honest and reasonable: he takes himself and, in the absence of contrary evidence, the player immediately beside him in the circle of trust.

Since mission one is where most games are decided by process rather than by hidden knowledge, I would rather we approve a clean, explained team now than stall and risk a rejection that hands leadership to someone else and gives us less information about how the rest of the table thinks. Omar, you have spoken plainly about why you trust Arjun, and that is the kind of transparency that helps a group of five build a working read on one another early. Arjun, you now know you are on the board, so I would ask you to play the mission attentively and report back anything unusual you notice, because the longer we run, the more that kind of observation matters.

If anyone sitting here believes they know something concrete that makes Omar or Arjun a poor choice, this is the moment to say so plainly, with the reason. I am not asking anyone to reveal private roles, and I will not speculate about them myself. Absent a concrete objection, my vote is to approve this team as proposed.

I appreciate the inclusion, Omar. Naturally, knowing my own alignment, I know I will be supporting this mission with a Success. Since we have very little to go on in Mission 1, taking a simple two-person proposal that includes the leader makes sense to establish our first benchmark. I'm ready to approve this team and see where we stand.

I'm comfortable approving Omar and Arjun for Mission 1. Omar gave a simple, honest reason for the pairing, and with no information about anyone yet, a two-person team that includes the leader is a reasonable first benchmark. I don't see a concrete concern with this team, so I'm ready to vote to approve. If anyone has a specific, reasoned objection, please state it now so we can weigh it before the vote.

Noah here. I still have no concrete concern with Omar and Arjun for Mission 1. The pairing is the simplest benchmark we can get at this stage, and Omar gave a clear reason for choosing it. Arjun has said they are ready to back the mission, and nothing said so far gives me a reason to hold the team up. I will vote to approve so we can get a real mission result and start gathering better information.

Elena again, briefly, and my position has not moved: I approve Omar and Arjun for Mission 1.

As a Loyal Servant I hold no private information about anyone's role, so my read on this table is built entirely from what I have observed publicly. What I have observed so far is that Omar proposed a plain, two-person team including himself, gave an honest reason for the second seat, and did not reach for the player he might privately know something about. That is exactly the behavior I would want to see from a leader on an opening mission, and it is the behavior I will keep watching as the game develops.

I also want to be explicit about a limit on my own claim. Arjun's statement that they would support a Success is not evidence of anything, because every good player would say the same thing and a lone evil player would happily say it too. I am not treating it as a signal, and I would caution anyone else at the table against doing so. The value of Arjun being on the board right now is observational, not testimonial: whoever goes out there can report back on how the mission felt, what the team dynamics were like, and how people behaved when they thought their card was hidden.

The thing I would genuinely change my mind on is concrete: a player naming a specific concern about a specific person on this team, with a reason I can evaluate, not a vague feeling or an appeal to role-suspicion about someone whose role nobody here can verify. No such concern has been raised by anyone, and I do not have one of my own.

With five players, a two-person team, and no information exchanged, holding this proposal up accomplishes nothing except burning a rejected team and changing who leads. I would rather we approve, run the mission, and start accumulating real information about this table. My vote is to approve Omar and Arjun.

Elena, third and final turn on this proposal, and my position has not moved: I approve Omar and Arjun for Mission 1.

I have said the substance twice already, so I will not repeat it at length. What I want to add is a note on what I will be doing with my remaining attention, since silence from me at this point should be read accurately rather than as endorsement of anything beyond this team.

As a Loyal Servant I still hold no private information about anyone's role, and nothing in this discussion has changed that. My read on this table is therefore still entirely behavioral: Omar led plainly, chose himself plus the player next to him in the circle, and gave an honest, checkable reason that anyone at the table could have offered for themselves. Arjun spoke once, briefly and without claims about anyone else. Noah, who has spoken at length, has consistently asked for concrete objections and named none. That is the entire sample I have, and on a two-person opening mission with a two-person team, it is enough. There is nothing to dissent from.

One caution I already voiced and will restate only because it is the most likely source of a bad mistake in this game: I will not treat agreement, confidence, or statements about wanting the mission to succeed as evidence of anyone's alignment. Every player at this table, good or evil, benefits from sounding cooperative in public, and a player who volunteers reassurance is not thereby more trustworthy than one who stays quiet. I am not asking anyone to read hidden roles into what is said here, and I ask anyone else to do the same.

What would actually change my mind, on this team or on any later one, is specific and verifiable: a player naming a particular player, a particular claim or action, and a reason I can weigh, rather than a general feeling that someone seems suspicious. Vague unease about a person whose role nobody here can see is not information, and I will treat it as such.

Absent such a concrete objection, my vote is to approve Omar and Arjun, and I am ready to move on to the mission itself.

Kenji here. I have no objections to this team, and I'm ready to approve Omar and Arjun for Mission 1.

With five players and no information exchanged yet, a two-person team anchored by the leader is the cleanest opening we can ask for. Omar stated a plain, checkable reason for picking Arjun, and nothing in the discussion so far has produced a specific concern against either of them. I agree with the point several others have made: vague unease is not a reason to reject a team, and I have no concrete worry of my own to offer.

I'd also add a small process note. Whichever two of us go on the mission, the rest of the table should pay attention to how the result is reported and how everyone reacts to it, not just the result itself. Early missions are mostly about building a baseline, and a calm, uncontroversial approval here gets us that baseline fastest. Rejecting this proposal would only burn a team and shift leadership without teaching us anything.

My vote is to approve.
Omar confirms Omar, Arjun. No concrete objection emerged, so I will keep the opening team and use the mission result as a starting point.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Kenji, Arjun. Mission 2 needs three members, and Omar and Arjun already passed Mission 1 cleanly, so Arjun is a reasonable anchor for a team. I am adding myself as leader and Kenji for a balanced, transparent three-person team we can all check against the mission result.

Mission 1 succeeded, but that does not clear Arjun or me: an evil player could have played Success. I know I am good, so I would prefer to keep Omar and Arjun together and add one player rather than replace me with two untested players. Noah, why did you choose to leave me off instead of building on the full successful team?

Omar, fair question. I left you off because Mission 1 already showed that you and Arjun passed together, so putting both of you on again would add little new information. With three seats, I wanted a team that tests a different combination: Arjun, who has a clean Mission 1 result, plus Kenji and me. That way the next result tells us something about the cards of the newer members, not just a repeat of what we already know about you two. This is not a judgment on you. One successful mission with you and Arjun does not clear anyone, since a zero-fail result is consistent with several possibilities. I am open to discussing a different third player in place of Kenji, but I would like to keep Arjun as the anchor and test a fresh pairing. Everyone should remember that Mission 1 cannot separate good from evil, so we should pay attention to how people argue for their teams, not only to the outcomes.

Noah, I understand the desire to test a new combination, but a failed mission would not identify which of the three was responsible. From my perspective, keeping Omar and Arjun and adding one player gives us a better chance of success because I know I am good. Mission 1 does not clear Arjun, but it is still the only successful pairing we have. I would prefer that team to the current proposal.

Kenji here. I support the proposed team of Noah, Kenji, and Arjun, and I want to address Omar's argument directly because I think it rests on a mistake.

Omar, you say you know you are good, and that keeping you on the team improves our odds. But the rest of us have to take your word for that, and every player at this table could say exactly the same thing about themselves. Your certainty is real for you, but it is not information the rest of us can use. What we can use is the structure of the proposal in front of us: Arjun carries forward a clean Mission 1 result, and Noah and I are fresh seats that will give us new information after this mission resolves. That is precisely what a second mission should do — test a new combination rather than rerun a pairing whose outcome we already have.

Omar's alternative — himself, Arjun, plus one — has a real weakness he hasn't addressed: if it fails, we learn almost nothing about who was responsible. Two of the three seats would be players who just told us they are certainly good, and the third would be whoever we appended. A fail on that team points nowhere. At least the current proposal spreads uncertainty across genuinely untested seats, so the result is legible.

I would also gently push back on the framing that leaving Omar off is a judgment against him. It is not. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fails, which is consistent with both members being good, one being good and one evil playing Success, or anything in between. Nobody is cleared, and nobody is accused. Swapping in new players on Mission 2 is the normal, healthy way to build a table-wide baseline, and rejecting a transparent, well-reasoned team this early — with a fail threshold that matters — would cost us a proposal and teach us nothing.

My vote is to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun as proposed.

I want to back up Omar's concern here. While it is true that Mission 1 does not guarantee either of us is Good, our pairing did produce a clean Success. Replacing Omar to introduce two completely untested players—both Noah and Kenji together—carries immense risk for the Good team. Kenji argued that testing two fresh seats makes the result legible, but the opposite is true: if this mission fails, we will have no idea whether Noah or Kenji was responsible, completely muddying our information. Introducing two untested players simultaneously gives Evil far too much control over Mission 2. A much safer, more methodical progression would be keeping Omar and me together and adding just one player, which isolates the new variable, or at least considering Elena rather than stacking both Noah and Kenji onto the board at once. For that reason, I am uncomfortable with this proposal and prefer we revise it to avoid taking both Noah and Kenji together.

Kenji again, and I want to respond to the pushback from Omar and Arjun, because I think the two of them are now making the same argument in different words and neither version holds up.

Omar, your core claim is that you know you are good, so any team containing you is safer than one that does not. I addressed this before and it remains true: your certainty is private to you. Every player at this table, including the ones you cannot see, could say the identical sentence. From where the rest of us sit, 'trust me because I say so' is worth exactly as much coming from you as it would be from anyone else. It is not a reason to hand you a seat over two untested players.

Arjun, your version is that putting Noah and me on the board together is 'immense risk' and gives Evil 'far too much control.' Look at what you are actually proposing instead: Omar, yourself, plus one appended player. If that team fails, the result points nowhere — two seats belong to players who have loudly insisted they are certainly good, and the third seat is whoever we bolt on. And notice something else about your preferred structure: you and Omar would then have occupied the exact same two seats on two consecutive missions. Whatever either of you is, that pairing stays permanently untested against new information. That is not methodical. That is insulation.

I also want to flag the pattern itself, calmly and without accusation beyond what is visible. Mission 1 succeeds, and the two members of that team immediately coordinate to argue that the next proposal — the one that finally tests fresh seats — is too dangerous to approve. Omar asks why he was left off. Arjun backs him within a turn and suggests Elena as a swap. Neither of them offers a concrete reason why Noah or me specifically should be feared; the objection is entirely about the abstract concept of untested players. But every player was untested before Mission 1, and testing untested players is how Good wins this game.

I have no private information about anyone's role, and I am not claiming otherwise. What I have is a proposal that spreads uncertainty across genuinely open seats and produces a legible result either way. Rejecting it buys us nothing except a burned proposal and more lobbying from the same pairing. My vote is to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun as proposed.

Kenji, final turn on this proposal. Nothing from Omar or Arjun has moved me, and I want to close by naming what their resistance actually consists of, because it is worth the whole table's attention.

Omar's entire case is 'I know I am good.' I have answered it once and I will answer it flatly one last time: it is not evidence to anyone but you. Arjun's case is 'two fresh seats at once is immense risk,' which is a feeling about a concept, not a reason against Noah or me specifically. Notice that across every speech, neither of them has produced one concrete fact about either of us. Not one. What they have produced is a consistent campaign to keep the exact same pairing — Omar and Arjun — on every mission board, indefinitely, while framing any proposal that tests new seats as dangerous.

And there is a new detail worth pulling into the light. Arjun, in your last message, you specifically suggested swapping in Elena. Why Elena? You told us the problem was abstract — 'two untested players together' — and then you immediately volunteered a named replacement. If the objection were truly structural, any single player would do. Naming one person, out of two available, is a specific preference, and it deserves a specific justification. Elena has done nothing at this table except argue carefully and transparently for the last two rounds. If Arjun has a reason to steer a seat toward or away from a particular player, I would like to hear it stated plainly, because right now it looks like someone lobbying seats for players they have a private view about.

Meanwhile, I am the one being told I am risky, and my position is fully public: I am an untested seat, I want to be tested, and I want Omar and Arjun tested separately from each other. That is the exact opposite of insulation. The proposal on the table gives Good a legible result no matter the outcome. Their alternative gives us nothing but a repeat.

I am voting to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun as proposed. The mission needs to happen, and the fastest route to real information about this table is putting fresh seats on the board.

Omar, one direct question before I sit down: if this team is approved, will you support it, or will you be campaigning against every proposal that leaves you off? I think the table deserves to know your answer before the vote.

Kenji, I will accept the vote and hope the mission succeeds, but I intend to reject this proposal as it stands. I would not oppose every team that leaves me off: my preference depends on the alternatives and the evidence available.

I agree that my knowledge of my own alignment is not evidence for anyone else. It is still relevant to my own vote. And a failed mission on either proposed team would not identify the culprit; Mission 1's success does not clear Arjun or me. I prefer adding one player to the successful pair, but I acknowledge that this is not a conclusive test either.

Kenji, to answer your question about why I mentioned Elena: it is simple arithmetic, not private bias. In a five-player game, there are only three players who did not go on Mission 1: Noah, Kenji, and Elena. If Noah puts himself on as leader, adding you means stacking two untested players simultaneously. The only alternative untested player to test alongside a Mission 1 participant would be Elena. It was not a special endorsement of Elena, but pointing out the obvious structural alternative if we wanted to test a fresh player without taking two at once. When two untested players go on a mission and it fails with a single fail card, the table learns nothing about which of the two is responsible. Elena, you have not spoken yet this round, and I would like to hear your perspective on this structural point: do you believe it is safer for Good to approve two untested players together as Noah proposed, or does testing new players one by one provide cleaner, less ambiguous information?

Elena here, answering Arjun's question directly, because it is the right question and I want to give it a straight answer.

Arjun, you framed it as whether it is safer for Good to approve two untested players together as Noah proposed, or whether testing new players one by one gives cleaner information. My answer is that the information argument does not favor your alternative, and I think the risk framing overstates the case.

Start with the information. You and Kenji agree the result of a fail is ambiguous, but you disagree about why. On Noah, Kenji, Arjun, a fail tells us one of those three holds an evil card. On Omar, Arjun plus one, a fail tells us one of those three holds an evil card. The ambiguity is identical, and it is identical for a structural reason neither of you mentioned: the only two seats in your alternative whose claimed alignment we could check are Omar's and your own, and both of you have said out loud that you know you are good. Every player at this table could say that sentence, so it narrows nothing for anyone who cannot see your cards. It is a claim, not a fact, and I refuse to treat a claim as a fact. I said as much in Mission 1 and I hold to it.

Now the risk framing. "Immense risk" is doing too much work. One fail does not end the game; Evil needs three failed missions. The real cost of a fail here is a spent proposal and a harder-to-read table, and that cost applies to both teams equally. If anything, adding fresh seats to a leader who has just taken a public position on the team gives us more to react to afterward, which is exactly what Kenji argued.

So where does that leave me? As a Loyal Servant I hold no private information about anyone's role, and I want to be plain about the limits of what I am saying: I have no concrete objection to Noah, Kenji, or Arjun, and nothing in this discussion has given me one. Noah's reasoning for the team was stated up front and has stayed consistent. Kenji has argued it forcefully and, so far as I can tell, accurately. Arjun has argued the other side competently but has not named one specific concern about Noah or Kenji that I can weigh, and I note that without treating it as evidence of anything beyond a disagreement.

My vote is to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. I would not have preferred two fresh seats if Omar and Arjun had been tested separately from each other before, but they have not been, and repeating a pairing whose result we already have is the slower route to knowing this table.

Elena, please consider the deduction from your own perspective as Good. You know your own alignment, which means the two Evil players must be among the remaining four: Omar, Arjun, Noah, and Kenji. Now evaluate the most straightforward possibility: what if Mission 1 was genuinely two Good players? If Omar and Arjun are both Good, then Noah and Kenji are mathematically the entire Evil team. By approving Noah and Kenji together, Good takes the catastrophic risk of handing Mission 2 to both Evil players at once. Stacking the only two completely untested non-Elena players onto the board together is not necessary when this is only the first proposal of Mission 2. If we test them individually—or ensure you are involved—we eliminate the chance of walking straight into a double-evil pairing. Given that a clean Mission 1 means Noah and Kenji are the two evils, does it really make sense to approve both of them together right now?

Elena again, and my vote has not moved: I approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. But Arjun, I have to push back on your last message, because it contains the exact error you told us you were careful about, and it is the whole weight of your case right now.

You wrote: "Given that a clean Mission 1 means Noah and Kenji are the two evils." It does not. Mission 1's clean success means nothing of the kind, and you said so yourself two turns ago, when you told us plainly that our pairing producing a Success was not a guarantee that either of us is Good, and that one Good and one Evil playing Success would look identical from the outside. You have now swapped a conditional for a premise. Your first sentence is a hypothetical — "what if Mission 1 was genuinely two Good players" — and then by the last line you are treating that hypothetical as established fact and calling it "the straightforward possibility." That is the step where the argument breaks, and it is the only step that makes it feel urgent.

Let me spell out the arithmetic that the rest of us are actually in. I know my own alignment as Good, so the two Evil players are among Omar, Arjun, Noah, and Kenji. Now take your hypothetical seriously instead of treating it as a fact: if Mission 1 was two Good players, then the evils are Noah and Kenji and your proposed fix would be correct. But if Mission 1 was one Good and one Evil, then exactly one of Noah and Kenji is Evil, and one of Omar and Arjun is Evil. In that second world — which Mission 1 cannot rule out — your preferred board of Omar, Arjun plus one appended player puts the confirmed-on-board pairing back out there while evicting the one player whose card we would most want to check. There is no version of your argument where removing both fresh seats is safer for Good across the possibilities we cannot yet separate.

And there is a pattern I want to name, calmly, because it is visible in the record rather than in anyone's card. Every speech against this proposal ends with the same outcome: Omar and Arjun keep seats. You argued to add one player rather than two; you named Elena as the alternative fresh seat. The result is a board where the same untested pairing runs again and the new information we wanted never arrives. The objection is always framed structurally, never about Noah or Kenji specifically, and it always resolves in the same direction.

My vote is to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. I hold no private information about anyone's role, so my reason for this is purely about the shape of the reasoning and the shape of the outcome: the proposal on the table tests new seats and produces a legible result, while the alternative repeats a pairing we already have and produces none.

Noah here. I am sticking with Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. Mission 1 succeeded, but as several of us have said, that result clears no one. The real question is which proposal gives the table the most legible information. Rerunning Omar and Arjun repeats a result we already have. This team keeps Arjun as an anchor and adds two fresh seats, so a Mission 2 result will tell us something new about the newer members whichever way it goes.

Arjun, I want to address your last message directly. You reasoned from a clean Mission 1 to the conclusion that Noah and Kenji are the two Evil players. That is a conditional, not a fact. You yourself said that one Good and one Evil player could both produce a Success, and Elena has already pointed out that the same logic cuts in more than one direction. We should not reject a team on the strength of a deduction that starts from an assumption none of us can verify.

Omar, I respect that you are confident in your own card, but I agree with the others that it cannot serve as evidence for the table. Your preference for keeping the Mission 1 pair is understandable, but it means the table learns nothing new. I would rather we have a team we can all read.

I am not asking anyone to trust me on my word. I am asking the table to judge the structure of this team: three seats, one anchored by a clean result, two fresh, and a fail that would be informative either way. I will vote to approve.

Noah here, and this is my last word on Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. I want to clarify one point in Arjun's latest message. Mission 1 gives us a conditional at best: a clean Success is consistent with two Good players, or with one Good and one Evil. Treating that as settled fact, that Noah and Kenji must be the Evil pair, is the step Elena pointed out, and rejecting this team on that assumption means rejecting it on something none of us can verify. I also do not think a team should be judged by who speaks most confidently about their own card. Omar's statement that he knows he is good cannot serve as evidence for anyone at this table, including him. This team gives us three seats: one anchored by a successful result and two fresh seats. Whatever the outcome, the mission will tell us something new about the table. I am voting to approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. I am not asking anyone to take my word about myself. I am asking the table to judge the structure of this proposal, which is clear and gives us a legible result.

Elena, third and final turn on this proposal, and my vote has not moved: I approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun for Mission 2.

I have made the information argument twice, so I will not restate it at length. What I want to add is a note on how the table should read the outcome of this mission, whatever it is, since I will not get another turn to say it before we vote.

The proposal in front of us has one seat anchored by a clean Mission 1 result and two fresh seats. That structure produces a legible result either way: a Success tells us the fresh seats did not fail us, and a Fail tells us one of the three holds an evil card without telling us which, which is the same resolution we would get from Omar and Arjun plus one appended player. Neither structure separates anyone from anyone else on a single fail, and no one should pretend otherwise at the table. The reason to prefer this team is not that it guarantees safety. It is that it does not repeat a pairing we have already run, and it puts new players on the board where the rest of us can watch how they argue and how they react.

One more note, addressed to the table generally rather than to anyone here. I am a Loyal Servant, so I hold no private information about anyone's role, and I will not pretend otherwise or lean on the appearance of certainty to make my case. Everything I have said has been about the shape of the reasoning, and I want that on the record. What changed my assessment, if anything, was not anyone's tone or confidence. It was one specific inference that was wrong on its own terms and was corrected by the table. Arjun, to be fair and precise about it: the sentence in your last message that a clean Mission 1 means Noah and Kenji are the two evils did not follow from your premise, and Elena's own arithmetic showed why. That was an error in the logic, not a sign of anyone's alignment, and I am not holding it against you beyond the vote. If I am honest, it also slightly raised my confidence in the proposal, because it showed the case against it had to be manufactured rather than drawn from what we know.

So my position is the same and it is simple: approve Noah, Kenji, and Arjun, run the mission, and then talk about what we actually learned from it rather than about what we assumed beforehand. On the next proposal, I will be interested in whether people have started naming specific players with specific reasons, or whether the arguments keep resolving into the same untested pairing. That is the distinction that will decide this game for us, and it is worth watching for now.

My vote is to approve.
Noah confirms Noah, Kenji, Arjun. I'm keeping the lineup of Noah, Kenji, and Arjun. It is a fresh pairing that tests new seats, and the discussion has not given me a concrete reason to swap anyone.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 fails (2 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Omar, Elena. Mission 2 revealed two fail cards on a three-person team, which means both Evil players sat on that mission and both played Fail. That publicly confines the evils to Noah, Kenji, and Arjun, and leaves exactly two players the result does not cast doubt on: Omar and Elena. As leader, the only team I can propose that cannot possibly contain a saboteur is those two cleared players. Anything including me, Noah, or Arjun asks the table to gamble the game on a 2-of-3 suspicion at match point, and it would rightly be rejected. Omar and Elena guarantees a clean Mission 3 result, protects our rejected-team budget for the missions that actually require difficult choices, and gives Good a solid success to build on. This is the transparent, information-safe play, and I will vote to approve it.

Elena here, and I approve Omar and Elena for Mission 3 without reservation, and I want to put the reasoning on the record in plain terms.

Mission 2 was a three-person team and it failed with two Fail cards. Two Fail cards can only happen if both Evil players were on that board and both played Fail. That is not a matter of opinion, it is arithmetic from a revealed result: with one Fail the mission fails, with two Fails both evils must have been present. Noah, Kenji, and Arjun sat on that mission, so both of the Evil players are among those three. Every player who was not on that mission is therefore untouched by the result, and Elena is one of them.

Now I can say something I have not said at any earlier point in this game, because it is now supported by public information rather than by assertion: I know my own alignment, and I am Good. I hold no private information about anyone else's card. Given that both evils are among Noah, Kenji, and Arjun, and given that I am Good, Omar is Good as well. The two-player team in front of us is two confirmed Good players. There is no fail card available for it, and the mission cannot be failed.

I want to say plainly why this is worth the table's attention at match point. One more failed mission is an immediate Evil win, and we have zero rejected teams on this mission to spend. A proposal that includes any of Noah, Kenji, or Arjun has a meaningful chance of failing and would end the game, and the reason is not suspicion or vibes about anyone's tone. It is a two-Fail result on a three-person team, which is the single most informative fact any of us has received in this game. Kenji read it correctly and proposed the only team that cannot contain a saboteur, and I do not intend to second-guess that by demanding more information, because there is no more information to demand. The only thing a different team could add is risk.

One small note for the record, since I would rather the table be accurate than comfortable: Kenji proposing a team that excludes himself, at a moment when a failed mission would hand Evil the game, is worth noticing. It is the opposite of what a player trying to lose would do. I mention it not as an accusation but as a data point in the same direction as the rest of this analysis.

My vote is to approve Omar and Elena for Mission 3. Let us run the mission we can actually win, and let us hold the rejected-team budget for a decision that will genuinely require one.

I approve Omar and Elena. The two Fail cards on Mission 2 establish that both Evil players are among Noah, Kenji, and Arjun, so Elena and I are Good. This team is safe.

For accuracy, we have one failed mission, not two: a failure on Mission 3 would not immediately end the game. And Kenji proposing this team does not establish Kenji's alignment; an Evil leader could propose a safe team in this situation.

Elena again, and my position has not moved: I approve Omar and Elena for Mission 3.

The basis is public arithmetic, not assertion. Mission 2 was a three-person team and it failed with two Fail cards. A single Fail card already fails a mission, so a Fail with two cards on the table can only mean both Evil players sat on that board and both played Fail. Noah, Kenji, and Arjun sat on it, so both Evil players are among those three, and Omar and Elena — who were not on that board — are Good. There is no Fail card available to us on this team. There is no further information any of us could demand before approving it.

I also want to record two corrections accurately, because the table should be building on what is right rather than on what is persuasive.

First, Omar is correct and I had it slightly wrong: we have one failed mission, not two. A failure on Mission 3 would be the second failure, not an immediate Evil win. My own earlier framing overreached. What remains true, and it is the part that matters, is that a team containing any of Noah, Kenji, or Arjun carries a genuine chance of failing, and the alternative on the table carries none.

Second, Omar is also right that Kenji's proposal does not establish Kenji's alignment. An Evil leader in this exact position could propose the same clean two-person team, so I withdraw any weight I put on that as evidence of anything. It is a data point about behavior only.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
